title: Nehemiah 3:15–32
context: The second half of the wall list continues from the spring gate past the city of David, the turnings of the wall, Ophel, the water gate, the horse gate, and the east gate, returning to the sheep gate where the list began. Several workers repair more than one section, and many repair near their own houses. Locations of gates and landmarks remain uncertain, and reconstructions vary. Both traditions read the list as shared ground about faithful, shared labor in rebuilding Jerusalem.

verses.text: Shallun the son of Colhozeh, the ruler of the district of Mizpah, repaired the spring gate. He built it, covered it, and set up its doors, its bolts, and its bars; and he repaired the wall of the pool of Shelah by the king’s garden, even to the stairs that go down from David’s city.
verses.arminianNotes:
Shallun son of Colhozeh, ruler of the district of Mizpah, repairs the spring gate and the wall of the pool of Shelah by the king’s garden, to the stairs from David’s city. The list moves along the southeast.

Arminian readers see careful work.
verses.reformedNotes:
The spring gate appears in 2:14. The pool of Shelah is often associated with the Siloam area, though identifications in this list remain uncertain.

Reformed readers see the city of David being restored. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: After him, Nehemiah the son of Azbuk, the ruler of half the district of Beth Zur, made repairs to the place opposite the tombs of David, and to the pool that was made, and to the house of the mighty men.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah son of Azbuk, ruler of half the district of Beth Zur, repairs to the place opposite David’s tombs, the pool, and the house of the mighty men. He is a different Nehemiah from the governor.

Arminian readers see another leader serving.
verses.reformedNotes:
The references to David’s tombs and the house of the mighty men suggest landmarks known to the first readers, though they cannot be located with certainty today.

Reformed readers see continuity with David’s city. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: After him, the Levites—Rehum the son of Bani made repairs. Next to him, Hashabiah, the ruler of half the district of Keilah, made repairs for his district.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Levites, with Rehum son of Bani, make repairs, and Hashabiah, ruler of half the district of Keilah, repairs for his district. Levites join the builders.

Arminian readers see those set apart for worship also sharing in the common work of the community.
verses.reformedNotes:
Hashabiah works ‘for his district,’ suggesting that districts organized their own contributions.

Reformed readers see sacred and ordinary service joined. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the whole people taking part, with each group contributing in its own way.

verses.text: After him, their brothers, Bavvai the son of Henadad, the ruler of half the district of Keilah made repairs.
verses.arminianNotes:
Their brothers, with Bavvai son of Henadad, ruler of the other half of the district of Keilah, make repairs. Both halves of the district contribute.

Arminian readers see shared responsibility willingly carried by both parts of a divided district.
verses.reformedNotes:
Keilah is named twice, once for each half district, in verses 17–18.

Reformed readers see order and cooperation among God’s people. Both traditions read this as shared ground about communities working together, with the list recording each contribution faithfully.

verses.text: Next to him, Ezer the son of Jeshua, the ruler of Mizpah, repaired another portion across from the ascent to the armory at the turning of the wall.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ezer son of Jeshua, ruler of Mizpah, repairs another section opposite the ascent to the armory at the turning of the wall. The wall bends here.

Arminian readers see work carried on at a difficult point in the line.
verses.reformedNotes:
Turnings and angles of the wall recur in this part of the list (3:19–25), though their exact positions are uncertain.

Reformed readers see diligence where the work was most complex. Both traditions read this as shared ground and hold the topography tentatively.

verses.text: After him, Baruch the son of Zabbai earnestly repaired another portion, from the turning of the wall to the door of the house of Eliashib the high priest.
verses.arminianNotes:
Baruch son of Zabbai earnestly repairs another section, from the turning of the wall to the door of Eliashib the high priest’s house. His zeal is noted.

Arminian readers see wholehearted effort singled out for honor.
verses.reformedNotes:
Only Baruch is described as working ‘earnestly,’ a small but memorable commendation.

Reformed readers see God noticing the zeal of his servants. Both traditions read this as shared ground and see in the verse an encouragement to wholehearted work, without speculating on why Baruch alone is so described.

verses.text: After him, Meremoth the son of Uriah the son of Hakkoz repaired another portion, from the door of the house of Eliashib even to the end of the house of Eliashib.
verses.arminianNotes:
Meremoth son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz, repairs another section, from the door to the end of Eliashib’s house. He takes a second portion.

Arminian readers see diligence extending beyond a first assignment, since he also worked at verse 4.
verses.reformedNotes:
Meremoth is one of several workers who repair more than one section.

Reformed readers see faithful service continuing. Both traditions read this as shared ground about perseverance in the work, recording without comment that some took on more than their first share.

verses.text: After him, the priests, the men of the surrounding area made repairs.
verses.arminianNotes:
The priests, the men of the surrounding area, make repairs. Priests from outside the city take part.

Arminian readers see priests from the region freely joining the Jerusalem work alongside the priests named earlier in the list.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase ‘the surrounding area’ is not defined more precisely, and interpreters offer different suggestions.

Reformed readers see the priesthood serving the whole community. Both traditions read this as shared ground about worship leaders sharing in the common labor of rebuilding.

verses.text: After them, Benjamin and Hasshub made repairs across from their house. After them, Azariah the son of Maaseiah the son of Ananiah made repairs beside his own house.
verses.arminianNotes:
Benjamin and Hasshub repair across from their house, and Azariah son of Maaseiah repairs beside his own house. Again homes set the boundaries.

Arminian readers see families caring for the part of the wall nearest them.
verses.reformedNotes:
The pattern of repairing near one’s home is practical and would also give each worker a direct stake in the wall’s strength.

Reformed readers see faithful service in ordinary places. Both traditions read this as shared ground and keep the observation modest.

verses.text: After him, Binnui the son of Henadad repaired another portion, from the house of Azariah to the turning of the wall, and to the corner.
verses.arminianNotes:
Binnui son of Henadad repairs another section, from Azariah’s house to the turning of the wall and the corner. The line continues.

Arminian readers see steady, persistent work along a long stretch.
verses.reformedNotes:
Henadad’s family appears again here (compare 3:18). The corner’s exact location is uncertain.

Reformed readers see each section joined to the next. Both traditions read this as shared ground about many hands contributing to one wall and do not press the details of the topography.

verses.text: Palal the son of Uzai made repairs opposite the turning of the wall, and the tower that stands out from the upper house of the king, which is by the court of the guard. After him Pedaiah the son of Parosh made repairs.
verses.arminianNotes:
Palal son of Uzai repairs opposite the turning and the tower projecting from the king’s upper house by the court of the guard, and Pedaiah son of Parosh follows. Royal landmarks appear.

Arminian readers see willing work near former palace sites.
verses.reformedNotes:
The ‘upper house of the king’ and the court of the guard recall the city’s royal past, though their locations are uncertain.

Reformed readers see the city of David being restored. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: (Now the temple servants lived in Ophel, to the place opposite the water gate toward the east, and the tower that stands out.)
verses.arminianNotes:
The temple servants live on Ophel, toward the water gate on the east and the projecting tower. The narrator adds a note about residents.

Arminian readers see the temple servants housed near the area where they served.
verses.reformedNotes:
Ophel was a district on the ridge south of the temple, though its exact extent is uncertain. The water gate appears again at 8:1.

Reformed readers see God’s servants settled near his house. Both traditions read this as shared ground and keep the topography tentative.

verses.text: After him the Tekoites repaired another portion, opposite the great tower that stands out, and to the wall of Ophel.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Tekoites repair another section, opposite the great projecting tower, to the wall of Ophel. They take on a second share.

Arminian readers see the common people of Tekoa doing more than their share, despite their nobles’ refusal (3:5).
verses.reformedNotes:
The contrast between the Tekoite nobles and the Tekoite workers is one of the list’s quiet lessons.

Reformed readers see faithfulness among ordinary people when leaders hold back. Both traditions read this as shared ground about willing service regardless of status.

verses.text: Above the horse gate, the priests made repairs, everyone across from his own house.
verses.arminianNotes:
Above the horse gate the priests repair, each opposite his own house. The priests’ homes lie near this gate.

Arminian readers see priests caring for their own neighborhood as part of the larger work of restoring the city.
verses.reformedNotes:
The horse gate’s location is uncertain, though it appears to have been on the east side near the temple.

Reformed readers see faithful service at home. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: After them, Zadok the son of Immer made repairs across from his own house. After him, Shemaiah the son of Shecaniah, the keeper of the east gate, made repairs.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zadok son of Immer repairs opposite his house, and Shemaiah son of Shecaniah, keeper of the east gate, makes repairs. A gatekeeper helps build.

Arminian readers see those with set duties also joining the common work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see each person serving according to his place. Both traditions read this as shared ground about ordinary and appointed duties working together in the rebuilding.

verses.text: After him, Hananiah the son of Shelemiah, and Hanun, the sixth son of Zalaph, repaired another portion. After him, Meshullam the son of Berechiah made repairs across from his room.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hananiah son of Shelemiah and Hanun, sixth son of Zalaph, repair another section, and Meshullam son of Berechiah repairs opposite his room. Some return for more work.

Arminian readers see continued willing effort.
verses.reformedNotes:
Meshullam son of Berechiah also appears at 3:4, and his family ties with Tobiah are mentioned at 6:18; the text does not comment on them here.

Reformed readers see faithful labor recorded. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: After him, Malchijah, one of the goldsmiths to the house of the temple servants, and of the merchants, made repairs opposite the gate of Hammiphkad and to the ascent of the corner.
verses.arminianNotes:
Malchijah, one of the goldsmiths, repairs as far as the house of the temple servants and merchants, opposite the gate of Hammiphkad and the upper corner. Craftsmen and merchants share the work.

Arminian readers see varied trades working together.
verses.reformedNotes:
The meaning and location of the gate of Hammiphkad are uncertain. The ascent of the corner suggests the wall’s turn back toward the north.

Reformed readers see God’s people united in labor. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Between the ascent of the corner and the sheep gate, the goldsmiths and the merchants made repairs.
verses.arminianNotes:
Between the ascent of the corner and the sheep gate, the goldsmiths and merchants make repairs. The circuit returns to where it began.

Arminian readers see the whole community completing the circuit, with ordinary tradesmen closing the final gap.
verses.reformedNotes:
The list ends at the sheep gate of 3:1, completing a circuit of the wall, though its precise route is reconstructed differently by interpreters.

Reformed readers see God bringing the work full circle. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the unity of the work.
